In brief

Parody. "The milkwhite dolphin tossed his mane […] and the bark clave the waves": after Bloom returns to the bar and is confronted by a visibly but unaccountably rancorous Citizen, Martin Cunningham moves to forestall violence by chivvying Power, Crofton, and Bloom onto the jaunting car that has been waiting for them outside. The car's departure from Little Britain Street is presented mock-heroically as if it were an enchanted ship setting sail, led by a faithful dolphin and power-assisted by water nymphs wrapped around the hull. The language appears to mock yet once more the Irish Revival mythology of a medieval past suffused with native glory, but if 19th century texts have influenced the prose style no one has yet identified them. Instead, this parody combines nautical terminology with fanciful literary images inspired by Shakespeare, and to some degree also Homer.

At more length

Joyce's narration employs nautical language—authentic, but not always accurately applied—to describe the ship setting sail. The "poop" deck, historically, was an elevated partial deck at the stern of a sailing ship, forming the roof of the captain's cabin. It was usually distinct from the quarterdeck just below it where the  "helmsman" steered the ship, but no such distinction is evident in the parody. The term "bellying sail" refers to a sail that catches the wind and bulges outward, like a round belly. Sails with deep bellies generate lots of thrust and are useful for gaining acceleration when sailing downwind. The narrative reports that the ship "stood off forward with all sail set." Standing off is a term for a ship keeping its distance from the shore or from another vessel. In this case the bow is being directed forward on its journey, away from land. Sails are "set" when raised to catch the wind, so the ship is deploying "all" its available canvas, seeking maximum speed.

Two more details, both quite strange, add to the impression of urgency. Among the raised sails is a "spinnaker to larboard." Larboard, the opposite of starboard, is another name for port or left. The term spinnaker, coined in the 1860s, refers to a large, big-bellied triangular sail used on racing yachts. They were unknown in the Age of Sail, but—since spinnakers, in the language of the OED, are "boomed out at right angles to the vessel's side, opposite to the mainsail, and used in running before the wind"—Joyce seems to envisage one being boomed out on the port side of the ship to complement its headsails, providing additional thrust. Speed is also increased by some sea-goddesses who draw "nigh to starboard and to larboard, and, clinging to the sides of the noble bark," add to its forward momentum

Although some of the details are fantastic, the essential message they convey is quite clear. Martin Cunningham has just said, "Off with you" to the driver of the car. He does not shout, but clearly he is eager to get Bloom away from the Citizen as fast as possible, and the parody makes it seem that he has commanded, Drive like the wind!!! A ship that not only sets all normal sail but adds a spinnaker off to the side is in a great hurry. The picture of this ship crowded with sail and helped along by animals and nymphs is in keeping with the chapter's usual principle of cyclopean exaggeration.

To this already fanciful account of the car's departure Joyce adds several mythologically inventive details. Dolphins sometimes race playfully alongside ships' bows, and he includes an especially picturesque one: "The milkwhite dolphin tossed his mane." There are several types of white dolphins in the world, but none have manes. This detail derives from an ancient Greek association of dolphins with mythical hippokampoi, "seahorses" that had the head and chest of a horse but serpentine or fishlike tails. Renaissance artists influenced by classical sources often depicted dolphins in non-naturalistic ways, sometimes involving manes and other kinds of flowing hair. One of the works of art reproduced here shows a dolphin with a flowing mane, and two others show them being ridden as one would ride a horse, with reins and a bit.

The milkwhite horselike dolphin is quickly followed by "the golden poop," a detail that apparently comes from the scene in which Shakespeare's Enobarbus tells his Roman friends about Cleopatra's captivating appearance on the river Cydnus: "The barge she sat in, like a burnish'd throne, / Burnt on the water. The poop was beaten gold, / Purple the sails, and so perfumed that / The winds were love-sick with them" (Antony and Cleopatra 2.2.191-94). Only the golden poop deck can properly be called an allusion, but other parts of Enobarbus's speech seem to have influenced Joyce's conceit. On the barge Cleopatra could be seen "O'er-picturing that Venus where we see / The fancy outwork nature," and she was fanned by boys who looked "like smiling Cupids" (200-2). Her female attendants, "like the Nereides, / So many mermaids, tended her i' th' eyes, / And made their bends adornings. At the helm / A seeming mermaid steers; the silken tackle / Swell with the touches of those flower-soft hands" (206-10). Classical mythologizing pervades the speech, starting with Venus and Cupid (seen in two of the Renaissance images of dolphins reproduced here) and continuing in the 50 semi-divine daughters of the sea-god Nereus.

Joyce's fancy of "many comely nymphs" who gather around the ship to speed it on its way may well have been prompted by these Nereids, and his dolphin too may come from reading Shakespeare. When Cleopatra mythologizes Antony, she says that "His delights / Were dolphin-like, they show'd his back above / The element they liv'd in" (5.2.88-90). Other plays deploy the Renaissance iconography of riding dolphins like horses: the captain in Twelfth Night tells Viola that he saw her shipwrecked brother ride a mast "like Arion on the dolphin's back" (1.2.15), and in A Midsummer Night's Dream Oberon recalls listening to the captivating song of "a mermaid on a dolphin's back" (2.1.150).

Still more details evocative of Joyce's ship can be found in this last play. Some twenty lines earlier, Titania has recounted how she and her pregnant votary used to sit on the sands watching merchant ships sail by: "we have laugh'd to see the sails conceive / And grow big-bellied with the wanton wind, / Which she, with pretty and with swimming gait, / Following (her womb then rich with my young squire) / Would imitate, and sail upon the land / To fetch me trifles, and return again, / As from a voyage, rich with merchandise" (2.1.127-34). Joyce's image of a helmsman who spreads a "bellying sail upon the wind" could have been inspired by this comparison of sails to a pregnant woman as easily as by Enobarbus's picture of the maiden at the helm of the barge who makes the silken tackle "Swell."

All of these resemblances suggest that Joyce imbibed a rich complex of images from Shakespeare—nymphs, dolphins, horses, ships, swelling sails—but deployed them in his own way. When he included sea-nymphs in his fiction he might also have been thinking of Homer. Slote, Mamigonian, and Turner report the observation of Harald Beck that the phrase "the undying sisters" resembles a passage in Charles Merivale's 1869 translation of book 18 of the Iliad. When Patroclus is killed, Thetis and all of the other Nereids mourn for Achilles. He tells his unhappy mother, "Would thou hadst dwelt with nymphs divine, / The deathless sisters of the brine." By themselves these three words might not seem sufficient evidence of an allusion, but they are preceded by what sounds very much like a Homeric epic simile.

Homer's similes illustrate features of the narrative action through extended comparisons. Many of his metaphorical images come from the natural world (e.g., warriors as attacking lions, or volleys of arrows as a heavy snowfall), but many others come from human craftsmanship: leather-workers stretching an oxhide shield to make the shield of Ajax (Iliad 7), Samosius's death resembling the fall of a tree that will be carved into a chariot wheel (Iliad 4), the beautification of Odysseus compared to a metal-worker's laying of gold on beaten silver (Odyssey 6 and 23). Joyce compares the nymphs' action of circling around the ship to the work of a wheelwright: "they linked their shining forms as doth the cunning wheelwright when he fashions about the heart of his wheel the equidistant rays whereof each one is sister to another and he binds them all with an outer ring and giveth speed to the feet of men whenas they ride to a hosting or contend for the smile of ladies fair."

Gifford, the first to attempt descriptions of the 33 parodic interruptions in Cyclops, has few specific observations to make about this one: "More parody of late-nineteenth-century romantic versions of medieval legend." Terence Killeen is content to second his motion: "The style is again that of a nineteenth-century version of a mythological story." Jeri Johnson does much the same, noting a parody "of 19th-c. translations of medieval romance." These attributions are quite vague. Until some scholar identifies a literary text of the sort the commentators hypothesize, there is no reason to accept their suggestion that Joyce was imitating some popular work of his own era. The evidence suggests instead that he was spinning out grandly romantic language—ending with the humorously antique-sounding "and the bark clave the waves"—from evocative motifs that he found in Shakespeare's plays, and to a lesser degree Homer's epic poems. Two parodies before this he wove a dialogue entirely from Shakespearean diction, and now he more grandly channels bardic speech. It is remarkable that no literary critic in the last century has detected the influence.

John Hunt 2026
